body:
Why cyber incidents matter

Banking, education, healthcare, electricity supply and government services increasingly depend on computers, communication networks and digital records. These systems make services faster and more accessible, but their failure or misuse can affect individuals, public administration and national security.

Consider a citizen who visits a public service centre to obtain an income certificate. The operator cannot access the government application. The immediate problem is that the service is unavailable. The cause might be a routine technical failure, an electricity interruption, a network problem or a deliberate cyberattack. The disruption must be examined before anyone concludes that a cybercrime has occurred.

This distinction is fundamental: a cyber incident is not necessarily a cybercrime.

Cybersecurity, information security and cyber incidents

Cybersecurity concerns the protection of computers, networks, digital systems and connected information against threats and harmful incidents.

Information security concerns the protection of information against unauthorised disclosure, alteration or loss of availability. It is broader than cybersecurity because information may also exist in paper records or other non-digital forms.

Cyber incident is an event that compromises, or may compromise, the security or normal functioning of a digital system or its information.

Cybercrime is unlawful conduct involving computers, communication devices, digital information or networks, either as a means of committing an offence or as its target.

A malicious attempt to steal passwords is a cyber threat. If an attacker gains unauthorised access to an account, a security incident has occurred. If the conduct satisfies the legal elements of an offence, it is also a cybercrime. In contrast, an accidental software failure may interrupt a service without involving criminal activity.

The 3 objectives of information security

Information security is commonly explained through confidentiality, integrity and availability. These objectives describe what protection is intended to achieve.

  • Confidentiality: Information should be accessible only to authorised persons. Unauthorised disclosure of a patient's medical record is a confidentiality failure.
  • Integrity: Information should remain accurate and should not be altered without authorisation. An unauthorised change to a beneficiary's bank-account details is an integrity failure.
  • Availability: Authorised users should be able to access information and services when needed. An inaccessible public-service portal illustrates an availability problem.

One incident may affect more than 1 objective. For example, an intruder might read confidential records, change selected entries and then make the application unavailable. It would therefore be incorrect to assume that a cyber incident can have only 1 type of consequence.

Incident, impact and evidence are different concepts

The incident is the event that affects a system. Its impact is the harm or disruption that follows. Evidence is the information used to establish what happened. These concepts should not be confused.

For example, an unauthorised account login is an incident. Disclosure of citizens' records may be its impact. Login records, notifications and related communications may help establish the facts. An unusual login notification is a warning sign, but it does not by itself establish who was responsible.

Cyber incidents as an internal-security concern

National security includes the protection of institutions and essential services, not only defence against military attack. A cyber incident affecting a public utility, hospital or major government service may disrupt daily life and public administration. The seriousness of an incident depends on the system affected, the information involved and the consequences of the disruption.

Individuals, organisations and governments therefore have related responsibilities. Citizens should recognise suspicious activity and report suspected crimes. Organisations should secure their systems and respond to incidents. Public authorities must coordinate technical assistance, investigation and protection of important infrastructure.

Prelims focus

  • Information security protects confidentiality, integrity and availability.
  • Unauthorised disclosure primarily affects confidentiality.
  • Unauthorised modification primarily affects integrity.
  • Loss of access to an essential digital service primarily affects availability.
  • A cyber incident may be accidental or deliberate.
  • Trap: A service disruption does not automatically prove that a cybercrime has occurred.

[Sources: NCERT, Contemporary World Politics, Class 12, chapter 7, Security in the Contemporary World, printed pp. 99-103; Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, National Cyber Security Policy, 2013, Preamble, paragraphs 1-7, especially paragraph 5. Official online source consulted 16 November 2026.]

title: Cyber Incidents: Meaning, Types and Consequences

body:
Recognising a threat before identifying its cause

A person may become aware of a possible cyber incident through an unusual payment notification, an unfamiliar account login, an unexpected request for confidential information or an inaccessible digital service. Such signs should be treated seriously, but they must be interpreted carefully. A warning sign suggests that something requires verification; it is not necessarily conclusive proof of an attack.

Early recognition is important because a person who acts quickly may prevent further account misuse, protect personal information or preserve details needed for a complaint.

Common threats faced by citizens and public offices

ThreatMeaning and warning signBasic protective response
PhishingDeceptive electronic communication attempts to obtain information or induce an unsafe action. A message may falsely claim to be from a bank or department.Verify the claim through an independently obtained official channel. Do not disclose passwords or one-time passwords.
Vishing and smishingVishing uses deceptive voice calls; smishing uses deceptive SMS messages. Both may impersonate a trusted authority.End suspicious contact and verify the request directly with the institution concerned.
Account compromiseAnother person gains unauthorised access to an account. Warning signs include unfamiliar logins or transactions.Use official account-recovery facilities, change compromised credentials and notify the service provider.
MalwareMalicious software may interfere with a device or information. Unexplained changes or security warnings may require examination.Stop unsafe interaction and seek assistance from a trusted technical support channel.
RansomwareMalicious software makes information or systems inaccessible and demands payment for restoration.Report the incident promptly and obtain authorised assistance; payment is not a guarantee of recovery.
Online financial fraudA person is deceived into transferring money or discovers an unauthorised digital transaction.Immediately notify the bank or payment provider and report the suspected fraud through 1930.

How impersonation creates risk

Fraudsters may claim to represent a bank, police authority, government department or well-known company. The claim is intended to make the recipient trust the communication and act without independent verification. The communication may demand immediate payment, personal information or account credentials.

The decisive distinction is between the claimed identity and the verified identity. An official-looking profile, message or telephone number does not, by itself, establish that a communication is genuine.

For example, a caller may claim that a bank account will be blocked unless the account holder immediately reveals a one-time password. The safe response is to refuse the request and contact the bank through a number obtained independently from its official records or application.

A one-time password, banking PIN or account password is a confidential authentication credential. A request to disclose it should not be accepted merely because the caller claims to be an official.

Recognition, verification and reporting

For a suspected deceptive communication, a useful sequence is to stop interacting with the suspicious request, independently verify the claim and report the matter if it involves attempted fraud or other unlawful activity. If money has already been transferred or an account has been misused, the response becomes urgent because further harm may still be possible.

Why symptoms can be misleading

Similar symptoms may have different causes. An unavailable website may reflect maintenance, an ordinary technical failure or malicious disruption. A delayed payment notification may be caused by a communication problem rather than an unauthorised transaction. A genuine incident may also remain unnoticed for some time.

Therefore, citizens should report observable facts: what message appeared, what action was requested, what transaction occurred and when it happened. They should avoid presenting an unverified explanation as an established fact.

Basic protective practices

Protective practices reduce risk but do not eliminate it. They include using strong and distinct passwords, enabling multi-factor authentication where available, updating software, verifying payment requests, avoiding suspicious downloads, keeping important backups and using official channels for support. If a cyber incident is already suspected, evidence should be preserved while protective changes are made.

Prelims focus

  • Phishing uses deceptive electronic communication to obtain information or induce unsafe action.
  • Vishing refers to voice-based deception; smishing refers to SMS-based deception.
  • Ransomware primarily threatens access to information and systems.
  • An unfamiliar account login may indicate account compromise.
  • Independent verification is safer than relying on contact details supplied by a suspicious caller.
  • Trap: An apparently official message is not proof of the sender's identity.

[Sources: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, National Cyber Security Policy, 2013, Preamble, paragraph 5; Ministry of Home Affairs, National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, Frequently Asked Questions, categories of cybercrime and reporting guidance, cybercrime.gov.in; Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Home Affairs, National Cybercrime Response Mechanism, 22 July 2026. Official online sources consulted 16 November 2026.]

title: Recognising Common Cyber Threats and Early Warning Signs

body:
Why prompt reporting matters

When a person suspects online financial fraud, account misuse or another cybercrime, the response should serve 3 purposes: limit further harm, inform the appropriate authority and preserve relevant evidence. Reporting is useful even when the offender's identity is unknown. Citizens are not expected to conduct their own technical investigation before seeking help.

The appropriate first action depends on the type of harm. A financial transaction requires urgent contact with the financial institution. Threats to personal safety may require immediate police assistance. Other cybercrimes can be reported through the national reporting portal and the police.

What to do after suspected online financial fraud

  1. Contact the bank or payment service provider immediately. Use a verified telephone number, official application or branch. Report the unauthorised or fraudulent transaction and request the available protective action on the account or payment instrument.
  2. Call 1930 promptly. This is the national cybercrime helpline, especially important for reporting financial cyber fraud. Give accurate transaction information and follow the instructions provided.
  3. Use the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal. The official address is cybercrime.gov.in. Supply the relevant complaint details and complete any further reporting steps communicated through the official process.
  4. Preserve the records. Retain transaction references, bank notifications, screenshots, messages, dates, times and any acknowledgement received.
  5. Cooperate with the police and financial institution. Provide additional information through verified channels when requested. Continue monitoring the affected account and secure access to it.

Contacting the bank and reporting through 1930 are complementary urgent actions. A person should not postpone one merely because the other has not yet been completed.

The role of 1930 and the financial-fraud reporting system

The Citizen Financial Cyber Fraud Reporting and Management System (CFCFRMS) operates under the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre. It was launched in 2021 to support rapid reporting and coordination with banks and other financial intermediaries.

When fraud is reported promptly, participating institutions may be able to identify or restrict movement of suspicious funds according to applicable procedures. This can help prevent additional transfers and may support the eventual return of money where the conditions are satisfied.

Reporting does not guarantee recovery of money. The result depends on several factors, including how quickly the incident is reported, the movement of the funds and the action possible under the applicable process.

The National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

The National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal (NCRP) provides a nationwide channel for citizens to report cybercrime. It accepts reports involving different types of online offences and has a particular focus on crimes against women and children.

Depending on the complaint category, the portal may request personal details, incident descriptions and supporting material. Citizens should follow the reporting requirements shown for the relevant category. An anonymous reporting facility available for online child sexual exploitation and abuse material and rape or gang-rape content should not be mistaken for a general right to submit every type of complaint anonymously.

Which reporting channel serves which purpose?

ChannelPrimary purposeImportant distinction
1930Urgent cybercrime reporting assistance, particularly for financial fraudIt is not the CERT-In technical incident-reporting contact.
cybercrime.gov.inNational online submission of cybercrime complaintsSubmission does not automatically mean that a police FIR has been registered.
Bank or payment providerAccount protection and possible transaction-related actionIt does not replace reporting a suspected crime to the appropriate authority.
Local or cybercrime policePolice complaint, investigation and action under criminal lawThe police perform the legal investigation; the reporting portal is not itself an investigating police station.

Online complaint and FIR: an essential distinction

An online complaint informs the authorities about suspected cybercrime and provides details for further action. A First Information Report (FIR) is a formal police record concerning information about a cognizable offence, registered in accordance with the applicable criminal procedure. A cognizable offence is one for which a police officer may arrest without a warrant in accordance with law; police may generally investigate it without a magistrate's order.

State and Union Territory law-enforcement agencies deal with complaints received through the portal, including their conversion into FIRs where required by law. Therefore, a portal acknowledgement number and an FIR number are not necessarily the same thing.

Two examples of the appropriate response

Unauthorised payment

A citizen sees a debit that they did not authorise. The immediate priority is to inform the bank and report through 1930. Transaction references and messages should be preserved, and the complaint should be completed through the relevant official process. The person should not wait to identify the fraudster before reporting.

Impersonation without financial loss

A citizen receives a message from an account falsely claiming to represent a government department and demanding confidential information. The person should not comply, should preserve the communication and may report the suspected offence through the portal or police. The absence of financial loss does not by itself establish that no cybercrime occurred.

Prelims focus

  • 1930 is India's national cybercrime helpline, especially important in cases of financial cyber fraud.
  • cybercrime.gov.in is the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal.
  • CFCFRMS was launched in 2021 under I4C.
  • State and Union Territory law-enforcement agencies handle police investigation and conversion of portal complaints into FIRs under law.
  • Trap: A portal complaint or helpline acknowledgement does not automatically constitute an FIR or guarantee recovery of funds.

[Sources: Ministry of Home Affairs, National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, Frequently Asked Questions and reporting guidance, cybercrime.gov.in; Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Home Affairs, National Cybercrime Response Mechanism, 22 July 2026, paragraphs on NCRP, CFCFRMS, 1930 and State/UT law-enforcement responsibility; Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Home Affairs, CFCFRMS 2.0 Platform, 28 July 2026; NCERT, Social and Political Life – III, Class 8, chapter 6, Understanding Our Criminal Justice System, 2018-19 printing, printed pp. 72-73, for the foundational distinction concerning an FIR. Official online sources consulted 16 November 2026.]
